provenance.method: Independent adjudication of every review-gated learner definition using catalog context and bundled WordNet evidence.

a1:00223465-r:behind.definition: At or toward the back of someone or something.
a1:00223465-r:behind.example: The child hid behind the door.
a1:00223465-r:behind.rationale: The physical-position preposition is the ordinary A1 meaning; the closest bundled candidate is an adverb and cannot support this prepositional definition and example.

a1:00252773-r:am.definition: The form of the verb be used with I in the present tense.
a1:00252773-r:am.example: I am happy to see you.
a1:00252773-r:am.rationale: The A1 source explicitly includes the be-verb, and that basic use is more useful than the unrelated morning abbreviation attached to this entry.

a1:02857998-n:pants.definition: Clothing worn from the waist down, with a separate part for each leg.
a1:02857998-n:pants.example: He bought a new pair of pants.
a1:02857998-n:pants.rationale: The clothes-and-shopping context supports the globally common trousers meaning; the only bundled candidate is the narrower British women's-underwear sense.

a1:03324991-n:fan.definition: A device that moves air to make a place cooler.
a1:03324991-n:fan.example: Turn on the fan because the room is hot.
a1:03324991-n:fan.rationale: The A1 objects-and-rooms context directly supports the air-moving device and is more concrete than the secondary admirer context.

a1:03370837-n:storey.definition: One level of rooms in a building.
a1:03370837-n:storey.example: Their office is on the third storey.
a1:03370837-n:storey.rationale: The spelling uniquely identifies the British building-level noun, which the bundled candidate represents; the entertainment labels appear to be source noise or confusion with story.

a1:03733928-n:match.definition: A sports contest between two people or teams.
a1:03733928-n:match.example: We watched a football match on Saturday.
a1:03733928-n:match.rationale: The hobbies-and-pastimes context strongly supports the contest candidate; the shopping label is too broad to outweigh it.

a1:03781824-n:mobile.definition: A portable telephone that connects to a wireless network.
a1:03781824-n:mobile.example: Please call me on my mobile.
a1:03781824-n:mobile.rationale: In British learner English, the ordinary A1 household-object noun is a mobile phone; the bundled database supplies only the hanging-sculpture sense.

a1:04414570-n:temple.definition: A building used for religious worship.
a1:04414570-n:temple.example: We visited an ancient temple during our trip.
a1:04414570-n:temple.rationale: The things-in-town context directly supports a place of worship and is more informative than the broad personal-identification label.

a1:09951098-n:coach.definition: A large road vehicle that carries many passengers.
a1:09951098-n:coach.example: We travelled to London by coach.
a1:09951098-n:coach.rationale: The primary A1 context is ways of travelling, which directly supports the passenger-vehicle candidate over the personal trainer sense.

a1:12648511-n:may.definition: Used to say that something is possible.
a1:12648511-n:may.rationale: The source lists a modal auxiliary as well as a noun, and possibility is the most useful primary A1 modal use; bundled noun candidates cover only the month and a shrub.

a2:00116161-r:physically.definition: In a way that relates to the body rather than the mind.
a2:00116161-r:physically.rationale: The body-related adverb is the ordinary A2 sense; the only bundled candidate is the narrower technical meaning concerning physical laws.

a2:00848000-s:plastic.definition: Made from a light artificial material that can be formed into many shapes.
a2:00848000-s:plastic.example: She put the food in a plastic container.
a2:00848000-s:plastic.rationale: The source explicitly marks the A2 word as an adjective, and the ordinary material adjective is more useful than the bundled senses describing moldability.

a2:01022875-s:handicapped.definition: Having a disability; this word is now often considered outdated or offensive.
a2:01022875-s:handicapped.example: Many organizations no longer use the term handicapped.
a2:01022875-s:handicapped.rationale: The learner definition should explain both the adjective and its current usage warning; the sole bundled candidate incorrectly defines disability as a noun.

a2:01897764-v:click.definition: To press a mouse button while pointing at something on a screen.
a2:01897764-v:click.example: Click the blue button to continue.
a2:01897764-v:click.rationale: The computer-interface action is the most useful ordinary A2 verb meaning, but the bundled candidates cover only sound-producing and figurative uses.

a2:02483951-s:organised.definition: Good at planning things and keeping them in order.
a2:02483951-s:organised.example: She is organised and always arrives prepared.
a2:02483951-s:organised.rationale: The efficient-planning sense used for a person is the ordinary British A2 adjective; the sole bundled candidate means unionized.

a2:04260861-n:max.definition: The greatest amount, number, or level allowed or possible.
a2:04260861-n:max.example: The max for this room is thirty people.
a2:04260861-n:max.rationale: The ordinary abbreviation of maximum is appropriate at A2; the only bundled candidate is an obscure drug slang term.

a2:05101152-n:degree.definition: A unit used for measuring temperature.
a2:05101152-n:degree.example: The temperature rose by one degree today.
a2:05101152-n:degree.rationale: Several everyday senses compete without source context, but temperature is a concrete and common A2 use directly covered by a bundled candidate.

a2:05815314-n:brainstorm.definition: A discussion in which people quickly suggest many possible ideas.
a2:05815314-n:brainstorm.example: Our team held a brainstorm before starting the project.
a2:05815314-n:brainstorm.rationale: The collaborative idea-generating event is the ordinary modern learner meaning; the sole bundled candidate describes a sudden realization instead.

a2:06339636-n:gender.definition: A person's social identity as male, female, both, neither, or another identity.
a2:06339636-n:gender.example: The form asks each person to state their gender.
a2:06339636-n:gender.rationale: The personal-identification context calls for the modern social-identity meaning, which is distinct from the bundled grammatical and biological candidates.

a2:09937051-n:fry.definition: To cook food in hot oil or fat.
a2:09937051-n:fry.example: Fry the onions until they are soft.
a2:09937051-n:fry.rationale: Cooking is the ordinary learner use and is represented by a bundled WordNet verb sense; the source's rare A2 noun assignment does not represent normal usage.

a2:10121403-n:footballer.definition: A person who plays association football, especially professionally.
a2:10121403-n:footballer.example: The young footballer scored two goals.
a2:10121403-n:footballer.rationale: British usage and the source's learner context indicate association football; the only bundled candidate is restricted to American football.

a2:15319328-n:float.definition: An object that stays on the surface of water.
a2:15319328-n:float.example: The child held onto a float in the pool.
a2:15319328-n:float.rationale: The travel labels are nonspecific, while the water-support object is the most accessible ordinary noun among the supplied candidates.

b1:00193263-r:continuously.example: The machine ran continuously throughout the night.
b1:00193263-r:continuously.rationale: The uninterrupted temporal meaning is the ordinary B1 use; neither bundled candidate clearly expresses it.

b1:00310732-n:safari.definition: A trip to observe wild animals in their natural environment.
b1:00310732-n:safari.example: We saw elephants during our safari.
b1:00310732-n:safari.rationale: Modern travel and leisure contexts support wildlife observation rather than the hunting journey specified by the sole bundled candidate.

b1:00994417-n:dating.definition: The activity of meeting people to develop a romantic relationship.
b1:00994417-n:dating.rationale: Romantic relationships provide the ordinary B1 meaning; the only bundled candidate concerns scientific age estimation.

b1:01277865-v:riddle.definition: A puzzling question or statement that has a hidden answer.
b1:01277865-v:riddle.rationale: The puzzle noun is the ordinary learner meaning and is represented by a bundled WordNet noun sense; the lower-level source row marks a less useful verbal use.

b1:01884326-s:rolling.definition: Moving by turning over repeatedly or travelling on wheels.
b1:01884326-s:rolling.example: The rolling ball crossed the road.
b1:01884326-s:rolling.rationale: Movement is the ordinary adjectival meaning; the only bundled candidate describes a trilled sound.

b1:08243899-n:crossroads.definition: A place where two or more roads meet or cross.
b1:08243899-n:crossroads.example: Turn left when you reach the crossroads.
b1:08243899-n:crossroads.rationale: The things-in-town context directly supports the literal road junction, which is absent from the bundled candidates.

b1:10786688-n:ward.definition: A hospital section for patients who need similar care.
b1:10786688-n:ward.example: She works in the children's ward.
b1:10786688-n:ward.rationale: The source category is uninformative, so the common hospital-section meaning is the most useful everyday candidate.

b1:13338024-n:customs.definition: The border authority that checks goods and luggage entering a country.
b1:13338024-n:customs.example: Our bags were checked at customs.
b1:13338024-n:customs.rationale: Both travel contexts support the border-control authority or checkpoint, not the bundled import-tax meaning.

b1:13347642-n:exchange rate.definition: The value of one country's currency compared with another country's currency.
b1:13347642-n:exchange rate.example: The exchange rate changed before our holiday.
b1:13347642-n:exchange rate.rationale: The ordinary financial meaning is a relative currency value; the sole bundled candidate incorrectly describes a service charge.

b1:14298742-n:gall.definition: Rude confidence to do something shocking or unfair.
b1:14298742-n:gall.example: He had the gall to blame me for his mistake.
b1:14298742-n:gall.rationale: The travel label is not reliable enough to justify the specialized horse-sore sense; the bundled rude-confidence sense is the most useful ordinary meaning.

b2:00801674-s:soaked.definition: Completely wet, usually because of water or rain.
b2:00801674-s:soaked.example: We were soaked after walking home in the storm.
b2:00801674-s:soaked.rationale: Completely wet is the ordinary adjective meaning; the only bundled candidate is the less common informal sense of very drunk.

b2:01575715-n:lark.definition: A small brown bird known for singing while flying.
b2:01575715-n:lark.example: We heard a lark singing above the field.
b2:01575715-n:lark.rationale: Both source notes are valid, but the bird is the concrete literal meaning and the selected bundled candidate covers the common Old World species.

b2:03082307-a:growing.definition: Increasing in size, number, strength, or importance.
b2:03082307-a:growing.example: There is growing concern about air pollution.
b2:03082307-a:growing.rationale: Increasing is the ordinary adjective meaning; the only bundled candidate means suitable for growth rather than becoming greater.

b2:04820120-n:dash.definition: To run or move somewhere very quickly.
b2:04820120-n:dash.example: I had to dash across the road.
b2:04820120-n:dash.rationale: Without source context several senses compete, but fast movement is an ordinary and concrete use directly represented by a bundled verb candidate.

b2:05039506-n:guts.definition: Courage and determination in a difficult situation.
b2:05039506-n:guts.example: It took guts to admit the mistake.
b2:05039506-n:guts.rationale: The broad food-and-drink label is weak evidence for internal organs; the bundled courage sense is the more useful ordinary learner meaning and common idiomatic use.

b2:08254784-n:cast.definition: All the actors performing in a play, film, or show.
b2:08254784-n:cast.example: The entire cast attended the film premiere.
b2:08254784-n:cast.rationale: The personal-identification and actor-hiring notes both support the actors-as-a-group noun, which is also the entry's original candidate.

b2:10484694-n:prefect.definition: A senior school student given special duties and authority.
b2:10484694-n:prefect.example: The prefect helped younger pupils find their classrooms.
b2:10484694-n:prefect.rationale: The education context specifically supports the British school role, which is absent from the bundled administrative-official candidate.

b2:12369152-n:ling.definition: A long edible sea fish found in the northern Atlantic.
b2:12369152-n:ling.example: The fisherman caught a ling near the coast.
b2:12369152-n:ling.rationale: No context distinguishes several rare homonyms, so the edible Atlantic fish is the most useful general-dictionary candidate.

b2:14470485-n:unease.definition: A feeling of worry, discomfort, or uncertainty.
b2:14470485-n:unease.example: She felt growing unease about the decision.
b2:14470485-n:unease.rationale: The ordinary emotional state is broader than physical discomfort and is not clearly represented by either bundled candidate.

b2:14980800-n:gook.definition: A thick, sticky, and unpleasant substance.
b2:14980800-n:gook.example: The machine was covered in black gook.
b2:14980800-n:gook.rationale: The idiomatic-expression context and sole bundled candidate support viscous matter; this decision does not endorse the separate offensive slur sense.

b2:82230893-n:corona.definition: The disease caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus.
b2:82230893-n:corona.example: The corona outbreak closed many schools.
b2:82230893-n:corona.rationale: The broad education context does not decide among senses, but this catalog-specific candidate and contemporary usage support the disease meaning.

c1:00682829-s:battered.definition: Badly damaged by repeated blows or hard use.
c1:00682829-s:battered.example: They found a battered suitcase beside the road.
c1:00682829-s:battered.rationale: The beat-up note directly matches the bundled physical-damage candidate; the cooking note lacks a corresponding candidate and is secondary.

c1:02168962-v:gape.definition: To stare at something with an open mouth in surprise.
c1:02168962-v:gape.example: Tourists gape at the enormous palace gates.
c1:02168962-v:gape.rationale: Both source notes are valid, but staring in amazement is the more frequent intentional human action and has a direct bundled candidate.

c1:04631874-n:physicality.definition: The physical strength, movement, or bodily presence that someone shows.
c1:04631874-n:physicality.example: The actor brought remarkable physicality to the role.
c1:04631874-n:physicality.rationale: The modern everyday meaning concerns bodily presence or action; the sole bundled candidate narrowly describes preoccupation with physical appetites.

c1:05832256-n:grounds.definition: Reasons that justify an action, decision, or belief.
c1:05832256-n:grounds.example: The judge found no grounds for delaying the trial.
c1:05832256-n:grounds.rationale: All three notes are genuine, but reasons or justification is the most broadly useful abstract C1 use and is directly represented by a candidate.

c1:09863364-n:batter.definition: A liquid mixture of flour, eggs, and milk used in cooking.
c1:09863364-n:batter.example: Pour the pancake batter into the hot pan.
c1:09863364-n:batter.rationale: The explicit pancake note strongly selects the cooking mixture over the competing baseball-player noun.

c1:10174170-n:hack.definition: To enter a computer system or account secretly and without permission.
c1:10174170-n:hack.example: Someone tried to hack her email account.
c1:10174170-n:hack.rationale: With no context and many archaic candidates, unauthorized computer access is the most useful modern learner meaning; bundled computer candidates do not cover it.

c1:14037117-n:recess.definition: A space in a wall set farther back than the surrounding surface.
c1:14037117-n:recess.example: The shelves fit inside a recess beside the fireplace.
c1:14037117-n:recess.rationale: Both notes are valid, but the architectural sense better fits C1 difficulty and is directly represented by a bundled candidate.

c2:00032610-s:acrobatic.definition: Involving skilful physical movements that require balance, strength, and control.
c2:00032610-s:acrobatic.example: The dancer performed an acrobatic leap across the stage.
c2:00032610-s:acrobatic.rationale: The standard gymnastics-related meaning is more precise than the sole bundled candidate's generic vigorously active description.

c2:02262825-a:seedy.definition: Run-down and associated with dishonest or unpleasant activity.
c2:02262825-a:seedy.example: They avoided the seedy club near the station.
c2:02262825-a:seedy.rationale: The source explicitly combines run-down appearance and untrustworthiness, so a curated definition accurately joins aspects split across two bundled candidates.

c2:03921038-n:perch.definition: A high place used as a seat or viewing position.
c2:03921038-n:perch.example: From her perch, she could see the entire stage.
c2:03921038-n:perch.rationale: Both source notes are valid, but the high-seat meaning is more generally useful and exactly matches a bundled candidate.

c2:05017985-n:echo.definition: A sound heard again after reflecting from a surface.
c2:05017985-n:echo.example: Her shout produced an echo across the valley.
c2:05017985-n:echo.rationale: Both verbal notes are genuine, but the reflected-sound noun is the foundational literal meaning and directly matches the original bundled candidate.

c2:05043392-n:athleticism.definition: Physical strength, speed, and skill in sport or movement.
c2:05043392-n:athleticism.example: Her speed and athleticism impressed the coaches.
c2:05043392-n:athleticism.rationale: Sporting physical ability is the ordinary modern meaning; the only bundled candidate gives the overly broad definition intense energy.

c2:07447159-n:dribble.definition: To move a ball by repeatedly bouncing or lightly kicking it.
c2:07447159-n:dribble.example: She can dribble the ball past several defenders.
c2:07447159-n:dribble.rationale: The basketball note supports the common sports verb and the bundled propel candidate, while the competing slow-pouring note is less frequent.
